Delivery Driver App Draft

This revised first draft treats your product as a focused native Android rider tool: drivers can register, wait for backoffice approval, sign in, go online, receive jobs from your existing website ecosystem through API integration, navigate to the shop and then to the customer, update delivery status, and review their daily work. The design direction follows the core rider patterns visible in public listings for 澳覓專送 and 美团骑手, while keeping the first version narrow enough to ship with strong performance.[1][5]

Immediate security note

The Supabase service_role key must never be stored in the Android app, and the GitHub personal access token should also be treated as compromised because it was shared in chat. Both secrets should be rotated or revoked before implementation begins.

Product direction

Your app should not try to be a full marketplace. The website you already have remains the source of business data, while the rider app becomes an execution surface for delivery staff: register, get approved, sign in, accept assigned work, see only the information needed to complete the run, open navigation instantly, and report status changes with as little friction as possible.

Primary user

Dedicated delivery driver who needs a fast onboarding flow, quick order context, one-tap actions, and safe navigation while moving.

Primary success metric

Shorter time from assignment to pickup, fewer missed updates, and fewer calls or chats to clarify addresses.

Core product principle

Keep the rider interface operational and lightweight. Every screen should answer either “what do I do now?” or “where do I go next?” and should render quickly on mid-range Android phones.

The best first release is a closed-loop dispatch app, not an open marketplace for gig riders. That means orders are created elsewhere, synced into your system over API, and then assigned to a driver or driver pool. The app mainly handles the last-mile workflow, while the website backoffice handles rider approval and operational control.

Phase-one business boundary

This app should not include any in-app payment flow. Payments happen offline between parties, and your platform acts as a coordination layer between shop and driver rather than a wallet, payout, or escrow product.

Reference signals

Public descriptions for 澳覓專送 describe a rider app connected to a dispatch backend, supporting order acceptance, actions across different order states, per-order statistics, and location sharing.[1] Public descriptions for 澳覓’s consumer app also mention that tapping an address can open search and route guidance, which supports a design where delivery addresses are always navigation-ready rather than plain text only.[2]

Public app-store descriptions for 美团骑手 focus on the same rider fundamentals: receiving delivery orders, managing order information, and viewing statistics.[5] That suggests your concept is on the right track if the first version concentrates on dispatch intake, active delivery handling, navigation, and performance visibility instead of trying to copy every surrounding ecosystem feature on day one.

Design takeaway

The rider app should look operational rather than consumer-friendly: big order cards, clear status badges, prominent map actions, minimal text entry, and strong attention to state changes such as “arrived at shop”, “picked up”, and “delivered”.

MVP scope

The first version should solve one clean loop from registration to approval, login, assignment, navigation, and delivery completion. Everything that does not directly support that loop can wait for phase two.

Must have in V1

Driver registration, document upload, approval-gated login, online/offline toggle, available or assigned order feed, order detail, shop and customer addresses, one-tap navigation, status updates, basic earnings summary, and push notifications.

Good for V1 if simple

Call customer or shop, issue reporting, proof of delivery photo, and a problem flow for unreachable customer or missing items.

Wait for V1.1+

Auto-dispatch optimization, batch routing for multiple active orders, heat maps, incentive logic, chat, rider wallets, in-app money movement, and full analytics dashboards.

Module Why it belongs in V1 Notes
Authentication Drivers need a trusted identity before they can see orders or location-sensitive data. Use app login for rider access, but integrate the website and middleware with shared-secret JWT tokens for server-to-server trust.
Registration and approval You need to collect rider identity documents before they can operate in the network. Registration should upload selfie, Macau ID, and driving licence, then enter a pending-review state until approved by backoffice.
Shift status The dispatch side needs to know whether a driver is available to receive work. A simple online / offline toggle is enough for the first release.
Order inbox This is the main operational screen and should open immediately after sign-in. Support both assigned orders and claimable orders if your dispatch process needs both.
Order execution Drivers need fast status updates tied to real delivery checkpoints. Keep the state machine strict so reporting and support are reliable.
Navigation The core promise of the app is to reduce delivery friction. Show both shop and customer routing as separate actions, not one ambiguous map button.
Earnings and history Drivers need trust in completed jobs and payout records. Daily summary is enough at first; it should show offline settlement records only, not in-app financial transactions.
Performance optimization Rider apps lose value quickly if screen transitions, order refresh, or maps feel slow. Native Android screens should prefer fast startup, list virtualization, cached order snapshots, and lazy loading of heavier modules such as map views.

Screens and rider flow

The app should be built around three frequent contexts: waiting for work, executing a current order, and checking results. That makes a four-tab structure enough for the first pass: Home, Orders, Earnings, and Profile.

Step 1

Sign in

Driver authenticates and the app restores current shift and active delivery state.

Step 2

Go online

Driver becomes eligible for assignment and starts background location reporting.

Step 3

Accept order

Order card shows shop, customer, fee, distance, and promised time.

Step 4

Navigate to shop

Driver opens shop routing first, then marks arrival and pickup.

Step 5

Navigate to customer

App switches to customer route, supports call and issue actions.

Step 6

Complete delivery

Driver confirms delivered status, uploads proof if needed, and sees earnings update.

State model

A strict order lifecycle reduces bugs and support disputes. The app should expose only the next valid action instead of showing many buttons at once.

State Meaning Allowed rider action
new Synced from external website and waiting for assignment or claim. None on rider app unless this is a claimable pool.
assigned Offered or assigned to a specific driver. Accept, reject, or timeout.
accepted Driver has taken responsibility for the order. Open route to shop, contact shop, mark arrival.
arrived_shop Driver has reached the merchant. Mark picked up, report delay, report issue.
picked_up Goods are in the driver’s possession. Open route to customer, call customer, report problem.
arrived_customer Driver is at the drop-off location. Mark delivered, upload proof, or mark failed attempt.
delivered Delivery is complete. View summary only.
failed / canceled Delivery did not complete normally. Submit reason and evidence if required.

Backend and data model

Because the business information comes from another website, the mobile app should not read that website directly. A safer design is to exchange data over API with a server-side integration layer, verify requests with shared-secret JWT tokens, persist mobile-ready records in Supabase, and let the Android app talk only to the rider-safe API surface. This makes permissions, caching, retry logic, callbacks, and auditing much simpler.

External website

Original order source. Creates or updates delivery jobs, receives callback signals, and hosts the backoffice approval flow.

Sync service

Server-side worker or API gateway that signs and validates JWTs, maps website data into your mobile-ready schema, and sends callbacks back to the main site.

Supabase

Postgres data, row-level security, storage for rider documents and proofs, and server functions.

Android rider app

Reads only the rider-safe subset: registration state, assigned jobs, profile, status updates, and proofs.

Amap SDK

Provides route display, navigation entry, traffic-aware navigation, and POI support.

External website ⇄ JWT/API integration layer → Supabase → Rider app ↔ Amap

Integration contract

Flow Direction Design note
Order create or update Main site → integration layer Use HTTPS API with a short-lived JWT signed from the shared secret. Include timestamp and request id to prevent replay.
Assignment and delivery status callback Integration layer → main site Send normalized status events such as accepted, arrived_shop, picked_up, delivered, and failed.
Rider approval result Backoffice → Supabase or integration layer Approval flips rider state from pending_review to approved; rejected riders can resubmit documents.
Document upload Rider app → storage API Upload directly to controlled storage with signed paths, then create metadata rows for review.

Suggested schema

Table Purpose Key fields
driver_profiles One row per rider. id, auth_user_id, name, phone, vehicle_type, status, approval_status
driver_applications Captures the initial registration and review workflow. driver_id, submitted_at, reviewed_at, review_status, review_note, reviewed_by
driver_documents Stores uploaded identity and licence metadata. driver_id, document_type, storage_path, verification_status, uploaded_at
driver_shifts Online/offline periods and activity windows. driver_id, started_at, ended_at, availability
shops Merchant pickup locations. external_shop_id, name, address, lat, lng, contact_phone
customers Drop-off destinations and contact info. external_customer_id, name, phone, address, lat, lng, delivery_note
orders Main delivery object synced from the website. external_order_id, shop_id, customer_id, status, promised_at, fee_total, source_payload
order_assignments Links orders to riders and assignment events. order_id, driver_id, assigned_at, accepted_at, rejected_at
order_events Audit trail for all state changes. order_id, event_type, actor_type, actor_id, payload, created_at
driver_locations Recent rider coordinates for dispatch and support. driver_id, lat, lng, speed, heading, captured_at
delivery_proofs Photo, note, or handoff evidence. order_id, storage_path, proof_type, created_by
sync_logs Tracks imports from the external website. source, external_id, status, message, processed_at
callback_logs Tracks outbound callbacks to the main site. order_id, event_type, endpoint, http_status, response_body, sent_at

Integration rule

The rider app should never own the authoritative business logic for order creation. A small integration layer should translate website data into a mobile-friendly order shape, normalize addresses and coordinates, attach assignment rules, verify JWT signatures, and handle callbacks back to the main site. That keeps the app simple and reduces accidental coupling to the website’s internal format.

Registration and approval flow

The login surface should become a combined login + registration entry point. On registration, the rider submits profile data and three required image uploads: selfie, Macau ID, and driving licence. After submission, the account stays in pending_review until the backoffice approves it, and the app should show a clear waiting screen instead of letting the rider into the operational flow.

Map and navigation

高德’s Android Map SDK supports map display, route planning, POI search, geocoding, and offline maps, which is enough for embedded map context inside your app.[3] 高德’s Android Navigation SDK adds route planning with real-time traffic, navigation components, and custom UI, which fits a rider workflow well when the user needs turn-by-turn guidance to the shop first and the customer second.[4]

That means the product can use a two-level map design: a lightweight embedded map on the order detail screen, plus a full navigation view for active driving mode. The embedded map is for confidence and confirmation; the navigation screen is for actual movement.

Because performance is a phase-one priority, map components should not be mounted everywhere by default. Order lists should stay text-first and fast, while the heavier map SDK should load only on the order detail screen or active navigation screen.

On order detail

Show shop pin, customer pin, straight-line distance, and buttons for Navigate to shop and Navigate to customer.

In active navigation

Show next turn, remaining distance, ETA, customer note, and one emergency issue button.

After deviation

If the driver leaves the route, re-open routing quietly and keep the status unchanged unless the driver reports a problem.

Important implementation constraint

Both 高德 Android SDK pages state that privacy-compliance methods such as updatePrivacyShow and updatePrivacyAgree must be called before using the SDK, and the platform also states that production or public commercial use requires proper commercial authorization review.[3][4]

Security and operations

The app will handle real addresses, phone numbers, identity documents, and live location, so the first version already needs a serious permission model. Drivers should see only their own profile, their own assigned orders, and their own earnings summary. Dispatch or admin operations should stay on the server side.

Risk What can go wrong Recommended control
Service-role leakage If embedded in the app, anyone can extract it and bypass rider-level permissions. Use only the public anon key in the app. Keep service-role access inside Edge Functions or your sync server.
Shared-secret JWT misuse If the shared secret is too broad or long-lived, forged system-to-system requests become possible. Use short-lived JWTs, rotate secrets, add request timestamps and ids, and verify issuer and audience on every API call.
Bad row-level security Drivers may read other drivers’ orders or personal data. Enforce RLS by auth.uid() mapped to driver identity and assignment records.
Sensitive document exposure Macau ID and licence images may be leaked or left publicly accessible. Store documents in private buckets, use signed URLs for review only, and keep review metadata separate from public profile data.
Unclean address data Navigation opens the wrong location or fails entirely. Normalize and geocode addresses during sync, not on the rider device at the last second.
Missing audit trail Support cannot resolve disputes about late or failed deliveries. Persist every status change in order_events with actor and timestamp.
Battery drain Constant background GPS hurts usability and leads to riders going offline. Report location at controlled intervals and only while online or actively delivering.
Slow mobile experience Drivers miss orders or delay actions if cold start, list rendering, or navigation handoff is slow. Use native Android performance patterns: lightweight first screen, cached home payloads, paging for history, image compression on upload, and minimal blocking work on the main thread.

If you want dispatchers to assign jobs manually, that should be a separate admin surface or internal web panel, not part of the rider app.

The GitHub repository you shared appears to be a Kotlin Android application with a single :app module, Android application plugins, Compose, Retrofit, Room, MQTT, and an Android manifest with a launcher activity and printer service.[6][7][8] It does not currently look like a web backoffice repository, so you may want to send the actual admin website repo later if there is a separate one.

Recommended next steps

The strongest path is to build this as a narrow but solid MVP. Start with registration and approval, staff-only or approved drivers, assigned orders only, JWT-secured API integration, and a reliable callback loop to your existing website. Once that works, you can decide whether to add auto-dispatch, rider pooling, heat maps, incentive programs, or courier batching.

Phase Goal Output
Phase 1 Validate the rider workflow Registration, document upload, approval state, auth, shift toggle, assigned orders, order detail, shop and customer navigation, delivery status updates, JWT/API sync, and callbacks
Phase 2 Stabilize operations Proof of delivery, issue handling, better earnings detail, support notes, push notifications, and backoffice review tooling polish
Phase 3 Improve dispatch efficiency Assignment logic, proximity ranking, multiple active orders, service-level dashboards
Recommendation

If you want, the next practical step is for me to turn this revised draft into a technical implementation package: Supabase SQL schema, row-level security rules, rider registration and approval schema, Android native screen structure, and the JWT-secured API contract with callback payloads for syncing orders from your website.
